title: +126% Since December: The Old Target Isn’t My Sell Signal
description: A higher target, less upside, and a war that changes how I think about this position. BUY maintained.
body_html:
A stock passes your target, keeps climbing, and more than doubles. Do you sell because it passed your target price?

Several subscribers have asked me that about the December energy pick.

It’s up 126%, and the price is well above my original target. If you have been following my picks for a while, by now you know that we encounter that question more than once a month…and should know my answer by now.

I’m keeping the BUY.

That doesn’t mean the opportunity is the same. I’ve raised the dollar target, but the remaining percentage upside is smaller. The business has delivered, the balance sheet has improved, and the war has pushed fuel markets far beyond the assumptions I used when we entered.

In this update, I revisit what I got right, what I missed, and how much of today’s profit belongs in a long-term valuation. I also explain why this position still has a job in the portfolio while the Iran war continues.

Table of contents

  • TLDR

  • How the stock ranks

  • What I got right, what I missed, and what’s evolving

  • The war changes the economics

  • What the latest results actually prove

  • The cash underneath the refining cycle

  • From $60 to $108: what changed in the valuation

  • What today’s price implies

  • The bear case and the risks

  • Verdict

Par Pacific Holdings [] is up 125.7% and I’m keeping it a BUY.

Subscribers have asked whether we should keep the position now that it’s far beyond my original target.

I promised an update and this is that update.

My revised model gives $108.30, compared with the $60 target in the December 16 deep dive. The dollar target is higher; the remaining upside has fallen from 54% at $39 to 23% at $87.

The original purchase solved a portfolio problem: we had no energy exposure and I thought the sector was undervalued as I explained in my most popular Weekly to date.

We now own PARR and National Energy Services Reunited [], which remain my preferred names for that exposure. The Iran war gives me a reason to retain it.

TLDR

BUY maintained. The position is up 125.7%. My target rises from $60 to $108, but the remaining upside is much smaller.

Three of five thesis pillars are confirmed, one is evolving, and one is challenged. Regional fuel economics, capital allocation, and logistics/retail cash generation held up. The original valuation framework needs updating, and I was early on the renewable project.

Q2 earnings were far above ordinary refining conditions. I include a strong 2026, then lower profits as margins normalize.

The model uses 8.2% WACC and 2.5% terminal growth. Recurring refinery exemptions and unproven renewable profits stay outside the base case.

The $73 bear case means 16.9% downside, against 23.3% upside. That’s 1 to 1.4 risk/reward; the BUY also reflects PARR’s role in our energy allocation.

Review the updated model here.

How the stock ranks

RankedStocks gives PARR an overall score of 95, with Sentiment and Outlook ahead of the other factors. You can use the site for free. The score fits the improvement in the business, but it needs to be read alongside the refining cycle.

Valuation. Low reported earnings multiples look attractive after the price doubled. Strong profits have lifted the denominator even faster. I wouldn’t treat today’s 3.8x EV/EBITDA as a multiple on ordinary earnings; my model deliberately brings those earnings down.

Profitability. PARR’s profitability factor is stronger than the large refiners in the refining peer comparison. Its fuel mix and local markets help explain that advantage. The FCF margin is less spectacular than its accounting margins, which makes the cash conversion worth examining.

Growth. The huge earnings growth rates start from weak comparison periods. Forward revenue growth partly reflects fuel prices. The negative longer-term EPS growth estimate is a reminder that consensus already expects normalization.

Sentiment and Outlook. Both support PARR, but refining peers also score well. Delek [] has the strongest overall score in this group; PBF Energy [] and HF Sinclair [] are close to PARR. PARR has stronger profitability than those three, while DK leads on growth and outlook. Its projected EBIT margin is also competitive with Marathon Petroleum [], Phillips 66 [], and Valero Energy [].

What I got right, what I missed, and what’s evolving

What I got right

Regional markets and fuel mix: confirmed. My December argument was that PARR’s locations mattered as much as its size. Four refineries, storage and distribution assets, and local outlets put it inside markets where replacing supply is expensive. Those assets still explain why I prefer this name.

Acquisitions and capital allocation: confirmed. PARR assembled that system over years, including the Billings acquisition in 2023. The important test was whether the assets would produce cash without continued dilution. The operating platform has stayed intact while management reduced the share count.

Shares outstanding have fallen 20% since Billings, and cumulative repurchases reached $351M by June. That increases each remaining share’s participation in future cash generation. Repurchases now require a stricter valuation test because the stock is much more expensive than when most of that reduction occurred.

Logistics and retail: confirmed. These businesses remain useful sources of cash alongside refining. They don’t remove the cycle, but they give PARR earnings outside the crack spread and support its debt capacity.

The return history also sets a limit on how much credit I give the operating improvements. PARR’s ROIC has swung sharply across the cycle, including a loss-making downturn and very strong profitable years. Management has built better assets; the business still needs favourable fuel economics.

What I missed

Renewable project timing: challenged. I expected the Hawaii project to contribute sooner. The August presentation places on-specification renewable diesel production in April 2026, after the late-2025 contribution I had anticipated. The facility is now operating, but I still need evidence of consistent attributable cash returns.

The JV reduces PARR’s economic share to 63.5%, while partners contribute capital and commercial access. Capacity and product flexibility are useful, but neither guarantees profitable volumes. I continue to exclude an unproven renewable earnings contribution from the base valuation.

I also didn’t predict the Iran war or the scale of this earnings surge. The December thesis discussed cheap crude potentially helping refiners in an oversupplied 2026. Today’s supply disruption is a different route to strong fuel margins.

What’s evolving

Normalized FCF and valuation: evolving. The higher valuation reflects stronger near-term refining profits, lower reinvestment after Hawaii’s turnaround, and an improved balance sheet, including the expected Laramie proceeds. The revised DCF lets those elevated profits fade toward ordinary conditions.

The tax advantage is also being consumed faster. The opening-2026 federal tax attributes were $700M, already below the $1B discussed in December. Strong earnings use those shields. My revised DCF uses a 25% normalized tax rate rather than extending low cash taxes indefinitely.

The war changes the economics

Oil prices drive much of PARR’s revenue because the selling price of fuel moves with crude. Profit depends on the difference between product prices and delivered crude costs, after operating expenses. A higher oil price can lift sales while hurting earnings if feedstock becomes expensive faster than fuel.

We need energy exposure while the Iran war continues and supply remains uncertain. PARR gives us exposure to regional fuel scarcity and refining margins; NESR gives us exposure to activity and spending by energy producers. They serve different purposes within that allocation.

PARR’s system has 219,000 barrels per day of crude capacity. Inland and waterborne sourcing give it several feedstock choices, but Hawaii still needs imported crude. The continental assets provide diversification when that waterborne supply becomes expensive.

The product mix helps. Management groups distillates and low-sulfur fuel oil together at 52% of output. That includes 38% distillates and 14% low-sulfur fuel oil; it isn’t 52% diesel and jet fuel. The combined mix gives PARR more participation in those fuel markets than the peers included in management’s comparison.

The EIA’s September outlook expects Brent to average $91 in 2026 and $74 in 2027, with U.S. distillate inventories below their five-year low through much of 2027. That supports near-term margins while allowing oil prices to fall later. I’ve used that $91/$74 price path as a forecast anchor.

Hawaii: strong margins, expensive timing

Hawaii’s Q2 regional index reached $46.06 per barrel, far above its longer-term averages. The refinery also benefited from $76.5M of contractual pricing lag as product prices fell relative to earlier pricing periods. Those contracts had hurt Q1 when prices rose quickly. I can’t treat the Q2 benefit as a repeatable improvement in the refinery.

Crude bought for Hawaii travels before it arrives, while selling prices follow different contractual dates. The war changes delivered costs as well as benchmark prices. August guidance pointed to a much higher Q3 landed crude differential, so I expect strong demand to coexist with less favourable sourcing economics.

Montana: execution alongside the cycle

Montana’s index also recovered sharply from Q1. Its higher Q2 throughput and lower unit production costs vs. a year earlier give me operating evidence beyond the commodity benefit. The coker’s planned July maintenance shows why the model needs maintenance spending and downtime even in a profitable market.

Washington: better economics without much extra volume

Washington’s Q2 index improved while throughput stayed close to the year-earlier level. That’s a useful check on the revenue story: PARR didn’t need a large increase in barrels to make more money. Better economics on existing production did much of the work.

Wyoming: a smaller refinery still needs cost discipline

Wyoming benefited from stronger regional margins, but its small scale makes outages and production costs matter more per barrel. A favourable index doesn’t automatically become distributable cash. I want each refinery’s captured margin after operating costs, rather than a single Gulf Coast benchmark used for the whole system.

This is why I don’t use my DCF as a signal while the war continues. It values a path of cash generation under assumptions about future conditions. Spot prices, shipping costs, contractual lags and fuel scarcity can change much faster than I update that path.

What the latest results actually prove

PARR reported Q2 revenue of $2.97B. Revenue exceeded the $2.4B consensus estimate. Higher fuel prices explain part of the sales increase, so I put more weight on profit and cash conversion than on the revenue beat alone.

Adjusted EPS of $10.10 exceeded the $8.22 consensus estimate. GAAP diluted EPS was $9.35. Both show a large earnings improvement, but extrapolating four quarters like this would build a valuation around unusually favourable margins and timing effects.

Q2 adjusted EBITDA was $571.3M, with refining providing $552M. One quarter therefore exceeded management’s $500M annual midcycle EBITDA estimate. That is how far current earnings have moved from an ordinary year.

The LTM reconciliation also separates inventory valuation, environmental-credit marks, and commodity derivatives from adjusted EBITDA. Those adjustments help assess operating performance, but cash available to shareholders still requires capital spending, taxes and working capital. I don’t value the stock by annualizing GAAP operating profit or adjusted EBITDA in isolation.

Management has earned credit for capturing the favourable market and completing major maintenance. The renewable project arrived later than I expected, and refinery interruptions still affect volumes, so I give more weight to completed operations than to an untested growth promise. September’s appointment of Jerry Stumbo as EVP of refining and logistics, with Richard Creamer advising through his planned retirement, makes continuity and reliability the next operating test.

The cash underneath the refining cycle

Logistics links the refineries to crude supply and customers. Storage, pipelines, marine access and rail let PARR adjust flows when individual markets become tight. That flexibility is part of the economics of the system.

Retail adds outlets and convenience-store earnings. Hawaii’s limited land and distribution complexity support the network, although Q2 retail EBITDA declined to $17.3M from $23.3M a year earlier. The business is steadier than refining, but its latest results don’t justify assuming that every segment benefits from rising fuel prices.

Together, retail and logistics generated $205M of LTM adjusted EBITDA. My model keeps logistics close to its $125M midcycle anchor and uses $70M for 2026 retail before returning to $85M.

Cash conversion is the larger question. Q2 operating cash flow was $282.6M after a $312.2M working-capital outflow and $19.5M of deferred turnaround expenditures. Management expects much of the inventory-related cash absorption to reverse. Its $614.3M figure excluding those uses isn’t cash already available for repurchases.

The expanded ABL provides room to finance inventory. However, a larger credit facility doesn’t create equity value by itself: cash released from inventory does. My forecast assumes inventory days fall toward 60; if prices stay elevated or sourcing requires larger buffers, that release can arrive later.

Net term debt fell to $321M at June 30. That measure excludes the working-capital ABL draw, so it isn’t the full amount deducted from equity value. The revised model’s balance-sheet bridge also accounts for inventory financing and other claims.

The Laramie asset sale gives that balance sheet another potential improvement. PARR expects $146M net, including $27.5M deferred for five years, and could receive additional contingent payments. I include the firm proceeds at present value, $137M, with no earnout. Closing was expected by year-end; I haven’t treated the announced sale as completed.

From $60 to $108: what changed in the valuation

My revised model gives $108 per share.

The operating business is valued at $6.2B, and equity at $5.4B. Laramie contributes +$137M: $118.5M at closing plus the discounted $27.5M due five years later. The other components are and -$86M to replace the model’s full-year 2026 FCF with its remaining half-year forecast. The resulting equity value is $5.4B, or $108 per share.

Near-term profit is higher, then it fades

The segment forecast uses $1.2B EBITDA in 2026, falling to $718M in 2027. Refining contributes $1.1B and $600M respectively.

For perspective, Q1 and Q2 produced $663M of adjusted EBITDA combined. The 2026 assumption therefore leaves $532M for the second half, less than Q2 alone. It captures a strong year while allowing for Hawaii’s turnaround, higher landed crude costs, and different pricing-lag effects. It doesn’t require every remaining quarter to repeat the latest result.

The $717.5M forecast for 2027 is still above management’s midcycle range. It assumes the favourable fuel market takes time to normalize. By 2037, segment EBITDA falls to $622M in nominal terms, $500M after removing the model’s 2% annual inflation assumption. A prolonged margin premium is therefore part of the upside case; the forecast isn’t already at midcycle next year.

Management’s ordinary year remains the anchor

Management’s midcycle EBITDA estimate remains $485M-$515M, including $125M from logistics and $85M from retail.

My DCF applies 25% tax and keeps recurring small-refinery exemptions outside the base case. The potential $170M-$340M SRE benefit shown by management remains an option on policy outcomes.

Reinvestment and working capital still consume cash

The model uses $205M of capex and turnaround spending for 2026, the midpoint of management’s $190M-$220M guidance. That’s lower than 2025’s $250M, but materially above the $125M normalized annual level. I use $145M in 2027 and gradually move toward normalized spending with inflation.

The capex reduction improves future cash conversion. However, maintenance doesn’t disappear after Hawaii: Wyoming’s next major turnaround is listed for 2027, Washington’s for 2028, and Montana’s for 2029.

The working-capital forecast uses 18 receivable days, 60 inventory days and 23 payable days. Lower inventory intensity releases cash as the operating cycle normalizes. That release is finite; subsequent FCF has to come from earnings after reinvestment.

The discount rate matters more after the rally

I use 8.2% WACC and 2.5% terminal growth. The improved balance sheet and the steadier logistics/retail contribution support the discount-rate choice. The 6% long-term debt-rate assumption is a normalization estimate; the newly issued 2034 notes carry a 7.375% coupon.

The 2.5% terminal rate allows modest nominal growth after the explicit forecast. It doesn’t preserve the war-period margins. Holding the forecast, terminal growth and equity bridge fixed, I recalculated the discount-rate sensitivity: 9% WACC gives $96; 9.5% gives $90; 10% gives $85. The $108 target therefore depends on the cost of capital as well as the operating forecast.

What today’s price implies

At $87, equity value is $4.4B. Applying the same equity bridge implies $5.1B for the operating business, compared with the DCF’s $6.2B.

One way to close that gap is 17% less present value from operating cash flows, keeping the discount rate, terminal growth and bridge unchanged. Another is a discount rate of 9.7% on the existing forecast.

Mr. Market has already recognized much of the improvement. The model doesn’t need rapid long-term revenue growth: revenue falls 14% in 2027 as oil normalizes, then grows only slightly. The remaining opportunity is in how much margin and cash generation survive, and what return we require for owning them.

At entry, the DCF helped me decide whether an overlooked business was cheap enough. Today, I also need to assess the energy exposure it provides during a supply disruption. A target based on normalized oil prices is less useful as a mechanical exit threshold while spot prices and fuel margins are moving so quickly.

The bear case and the risks

The model’s $73 bear case gives 16.9% downside with 23.3% upside, so risk/reward is 1 to 1.4. A weaker outcome could combine faster crack-spread normalization, delayed inventory cash release, and a higher required return. The discount-rate sensitivity already shows how much of the base-case upside disappears without an operating collapse.

Commodity and geopolitical risk has materialized. Hawaii’s opposite Q1 and Q2 price-lag effects show how volatility reaches the accounts. If the war ends and product scarcity eases, profits can fall. If crude supply tightens faster than fuel prices rise, margins can also suffer while the war continues. The duration of the conflict alone can’t guarantee a profitable refinery.

Operational and Hawaii concentration risks remain. A refinery that can’t run doesn’t capture the attractive market. In the next results, I’ll watch Hawaii’s throughput, delivered crude costs and margin capture, plus Montana’s coker performance. A missed quarter during scarce supply has a greater cash cost because the lost barrels could have been unusually profitable.

Near-term refinancing risk has faded, but cash allocation still matters. Lower term debt, extended facilities and the prospective Laramie proceeds improve flexibility. The next test is whether the strong earnings become cash and whether management buys back stock at a price that improves per-share value.

Policy and renewable risks remain, with a timing miss already visible. The base case excludes repeat SRE windfalls and unproven renewable profits. That prevents either from being essential to $108, but it doesn’t eliminate ordinary compliance costs, ramp expenses, or the risk that the project earns less than expected.

Verdict

PARR remains a BUY, with a $108 target. I’m keeping it alongside NESR because they remain my preferred energy exposures while the Iran war continues, and PARR’s local fuel economics and cash generation still support the position. I’ll revisit that call if those economics weaken or the price outruns what they can support.
